Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- Summary of assessment findings from transcript and DDx where consistent:
  • 50-year-old female with six days of dysuria, midline suprapubic pain (7/10), foul-smelling urine, and hematuria (blood spots in urine). No fever. Able to pass urine. Regular menses. IBS history. On mebeverine. Allergic to clindamycin. Hydration and symptomatic management discussed.
- Likely diagnoses (DDx aligned with transcript):
  • Acute cystitis (lower urinary tract infection) – High
  • Nephrolithiasis (urinary stone) – Medium
  • Pyelonephritis (upper urinary tract infection) – Medium
  • Bladder cancer (urothelial carcinoma) – Low
- Notes on consistency or conflict: No conflicts noted with transcript; DDx aligns with clinical picture and empiric treatment plan.

Management Plan
- management_plan_main: Empiric antibiotic therapy for presumed acute cystitis (3-day course) with prescription to Knightsbridge pharmacy; start after pickup (approximately 1 hour). Advise increased fluid intake (2.5–3 litres/day). Recommend cranberry juice and urine-acidity sachets to help modify urine pH. Educate on red flags: worsening pain, fever, back/loin pain, or difficulty passing urine; contact provider promptly if symptoms worsen or do not resolve. If symptoms recur or become a recurrent issue, reevaluate.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Acute cystitis (lower UTI) – High
  - Justification: Dysuria, foul-smelling urine, suprapubic pain, and hematuria with no fever; treatment plan consistent with uncomplicated cystitis.
- Nephrolithiasis (urinary stone) – Medium
  - Justification: Hematuria and acute abdominal pain; pain severity; however presentation lacks classic flank/loin pain and radiating features.
- Pyelonephritis (upper UTI) – Medium
  - Justification: Infectious urinary symptoms; absence of fever or flank tenderness; still plausible in early or atypical presentations.
- Bladder cancer (urothelial carcinoma) – Low
  - Justification: Hematuria in age >50 warrants consideration, but acute infectious presentation and response to short antibiotic therapy reduce likelihood as primary etiology.
